source_user: Advanced cluster case Mooncake-100: Analyze Mooncake-style disaggregated KV-cache or serving architecture for a long-context workload. Variant 100 must state assumptions, define a falsifiable hypothesis, name metrics, and include one failure or rollback condition.
source_assistant: An expert answer should distinguish model-domain mechanisms from runtime measurements. Required technical anchors: define prefill/decode ownership, KV placement and eviction, RDMA transfer cost, cache consistency, admission control, failure recovery, and comparison against local or conventional distributed serving. It must report topology, workload, units, baselines, confounders, and evidence needed before claiming improvement.
corrected_answer:
Use a read-only, auditable diagnostic workflow before changing configuration or attributing a fault to RDMA. Assume a multi-node long-context service, but do not infer platform facts: record model/runtime versions, GPU and NIC models, PCIe/NUMA affinity, RDMA device and link capabilities, memory limits, topology and failure domains, prompt and generation-length distributions, concurrency, batching, cache warmness, and tenant policy. Unknowns are evidence_required. This is Mooncake variant 100; separate model-domain mechanisms from runtime measurements.

Make ownership explicit: prefill workers construct KV and decode workers consume it. Specify the block schema and precision, token-position and model/revision cache key, namespace, placement, replication, leases/epochs, version and checksum validation, TTL, eviction priority, admission quotas, and control-plane commit states. Authorize and enforce tenant isolation before lookup. Reject stale, partial, corrupt, mismatched, or unauthorized blocks; never silently use them. On misses, RDMA timeout/link error, node loss, or control-plane inconsistency, use bounded timeout and retry budgets, recompute locally or use conventional serving, and preserve correctness. Define idempotent writes, fencing for failed owners, replica health checks, and a rollback gate that disables remote reuse if error rate, data-integrity failures, or tail latency exceeds the predeclared threshold.

Falsifiable hypothesis: for a specified prompt-length/concurrency mix and SLO, remote KV lowers decode startup or end-to-end p95/p99 latency and/or increases useful throughput without changing output correctness, compared with a local-KV baseline and a conventional distributed-serving baseline. Measure TTFT, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency, throughput (requests/s and tokens/s), KV hit rate, bytes transferred, RDMA operations, transfer time, GPU utilization, memory occupancy, queueing, retries, fallback rate, error rate, and p50/p95/p99 with units. Use repeated randomized runs after a declared warm-up, matched batching and load, confidence intervals, and output-equivalence checks. Attribute RDMA cost separately from prefill, serialization, PCIe/NUMA copies, decode, queueing, and control-plane work; report topology, link utilization, offered load, cache state, and failure-injection results. Confounders include prompt mix, sequence lengths, scheduling, replication, compression/precision, competing traffic, and thermal or resource contention. Do not claim improvement until the measured data and failure evidence support it; record rollback and recovery observations.
risks: platform-specific capabilities may be unavailable or differ from assumptions
remote KV can amplify tail latency or serve stale/corrupt data if validation and fencing are incomplete
failure-injection and output-equivalence evidence is required before deployment
evidence_required: actual topology, GPU/NIC/RDMA and NUMA inventory
matched local and conventional-serving baselines with repeated latency/throughput measurements
KV schema/version/checksum and authorization tests
node/link/control-plane failure-injection results and rollback observations
